Method #1 (easiest)

Grab the minified css and paste it into the custom stylesheet box in subverse settings. A perfectly good option if you don't want to customize anything.

 

Method #2 (best)

Download the SCSS files and edit them on your computer, processing them with Sass. This is how Cashmere is developed and ideally intended to be used. You will need to have Sass installed. Sass can be used through the command-line or with a third-party graphical application. Cashmere is designed to be highly customizable, even for those unfamiliar with Sass. Here's a basic guide for setting the colours.

 

Method #3 (easy-ish)

You can still use the SCSS, even without installing Sass, by using an online Sass compiler such as sassmeister.com or codepen.io. Simply copy and paste the contents of cashmere.cat.scss, make your changes, and get the CSS output. I highly recommend installing Sass locally, but I recognize this can be intimidating to some, so this is also an option. It might be sluggish, but it'll get the job done.

Check out Koala. It's a very simple GUI that compiles Sass (and other CSS preprocessors). Notepad++ should work fine.

You can include your additional stylesheet as CSS or SCSS, but I'd recommend _example.scss (the underscore at the beginning tells Sass not to make a seperate output file for it). Just because the file is .scss, doesn't mean you actually have to use any SCSS stuff. You can put normal CSS in it and it will work fine. You also have to add this file to cashmere.scss. @import should be self-explanatory by looking at the other lines. There's no underscore in the @import path. The file path is relative to cashmere.scss.

Once you have Koala set up for your project, it will create a single file with Cashmere and your custom styles every time you save any file in the project directory.

I'm going to try explaining this from the beginning to the best of my ability. It should not be necessary to use the command line.

  1. Download Cashmere and unzip it.

  2. Go into the folder scss/. This is the only folder you need.

  3. Delete cashmere.cat.scss because you won't need that.

  4. Create a new empty document called _extrastuff.scss.

  5. Open cashmere.scss and add this line to the bottom: @import 'extrastuff';.

  6. Open Koala and it will ask you to drag a folder into it. Drag in the folder scss/. Koala should now be configured correctly.

  7. Open _extrastuff.scss in your preferred text editor and add your code. Pure CSS and SCSS will both work.

  8. Save _extrastuff.scss and Koala should automatically process everything and produce a file called cashmere.css. You can now copy the contents of this file into your subverse settings.

From what I understand, Koala has its own copy of Ruby installed, so I don't think you need the command line at all.

Here's the Koala documentation.

There's not really any such thing as 'believing' in science.

Most broadly, belief is just acceptance that something is true. David Hume famously wrote, "A wise man apportions his beliefs to the evidence." That's exactly the kind of belief that is appropriate in science. I understand that many people feel that the word 'belief' has been tainted by religious connotations, but contrary to what you claim about ignorance, it is not that unusual to come across the word 'believe' used in a generic sense to mean, 'are convinced that' in the scientific literature.

Strictly speaking what you said about 'believing' is true, but I feel it has a role from a pragmatic perspective. We're used to seeing studies published that contradict the conventional wisdom. As scientists, we should be sceptics (fuck the climate politics that has poisoned that word), so just because one group has got a result does not mean that we should accept it as fact. As other groups begin to duplicate a result and build on it, the body of evidence grows, and there comes a point where we are all swayed from being sceptically optimistic (disbelieving) to accepting the result (believing). Where that point is depends on a number of factors (how significant the contradiction is, which research group/country published the result, what we personally conjecture about the topic, etc.).
My heart hopes it works but my head is doubtful that there isn't something else going on here.

It's been confirmed by multiple labs who have 100% access to the device (so no possibility of shenanigans like certain controversial seemingly bullshit devices). But we have no idea how it works. About the only thing we can say for sure is that it doesn't work the way the inventor thought it did, because NASA ran a sabotaged test that would have kept it from working if the guy was right.

Some ways it might work will make it either useless or minimally useful for space travel, it could be interacting with air (the vacuum chamber test wasn't actually in vacuum, they stuck it in there real fast to eliminate the possibility of micro-currents) in which case it will be useless in space, or it could be interacting with the magnetic field, in which case it won't work outside of LEO.

Some recent (still unpublished not yet reliable!) experiments NASA did indicate it could be a badly functioning warp drive, and in that case yes it would work, as well as providing good evidence of how to make the Alcubierre drive actually work (last I checked, NASA had gotten as far as 'we can't prove its impossible', so showing the effect exists would be a big deal).

I'm nearly completely certain that it cannot work. The nomaly should definitely be looked into, we're going to learn something no matter what we find. But this won't turn into a practical method of propulsion. Physics has this nasty habit of not wanting to be violated, no matter how hard you try.

From a practical point of view, it's great because it generates thrust without need for a reaction mass (i.e. in space flight it doesn't need a propellant).
